utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, technical booth; good morning, interpreters; good morning, legal assistants, court reporters; good morning, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey; good morning, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic. Good morning to the expert. Good morning, Dr. Clark, have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to resume our hearing. I should like to remind you, Mr. Clark, that you are continuing to testify under oath, and you're going to continue to answer questions put to you by Mr. Cayley. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Cayley: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, just to remind you what I said yesterday, as we speak the same language, if you could try and take a pause between question and answer. I'll do the same, and I'll try to regulate the pace. That will make the interpreters' lives easier. We reached, I think, yesterday, the conclusions that you made in respect of the bodies that were recovered from the Kozluk grave. So now if we could move on to the bodies and body parts that were recovered from Nova Kasaba. Do you have that page of your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies and body parts, Dr. Clark, were found or were recovered and presented to you from that site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifty-five bodies and two small body parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in life, what kind of people were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people, again, with a wide age range. The estimate ranges potentially as young as 13, potentially as old at 85 or even older. Most of them appeared to be over the age of 25. As far as we could tell, all were male. They appear to be a reasonably fit population. One person had an old fracture of his leg, and somebody -- another one an old injury of his right hand, but these were injuries from years past. We didn't have the same disabilities or deformities as we had in the bodies at Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the cause of death in the majority of the cases from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the majority of people died from gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other evidence concerning any other weapons that might have been used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, interestingly. The bulk of the people who had been shot appeared to have been shot by high-velocity rifles, as in Kozluk, but in one person, the hole -- the wound in the bone appeared -- it suggested to us possibly the use of a handgun, and in five cases there was clear evidence of shotgun pellets in the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could place Exhibit 246. This was something of particular interest from this site, and if you could describe to the Judges your findings in respect of this particular body.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two men who had recent injuries to them, and I'm meaning injuries possibly in the few days before the death. These were both men with gunshot injuries to the legs, and we could tell that they hadn't occurred right at the time of death because they had been bandaged up. This example here, you're seeing the lower part of the man's body. This is his left leg here, and clearly it has a splint and bandages around it. So this is clearly an injury that he has -- had suffered, gunshot injury, that has had time to have been bandaged up. And there was a second man with a fairly similar injury to his leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If you'd place the next exhibit on the ELMO, which I think is a close-up shot of the same.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is just a close-up shot in amongst the bandages, just to show the gunshot wound in his leg. This body was fairly well preserved. There was skin and some soft tissue, so it was still possible to see a hole in the skin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, if you could place Exhibit 248. I think the next three photographs demonstrate some of the classical injuries that you observed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the back of a skull with two bullet holes in the back of it. Interestingly, these do not have the typical pattern of high-velocity weapons with the shattering, so this may well have been a handgun injury. The other two photographs I have just to show that there were injuries to parts of the body other than the head. This is a rib. You see a very clear bullet hole going through it. And finally, a typical injury from somebody's leg. This is the thigh bone, and the bone here is shattered and in many pieces, and very typical of a bullet coming from this direction, shattering the bone in that way, a very typical high-velocity injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for purposes of the record, when Dr. Clark was referring to a bullet injury to a rib, that is Prosecutor's Exhibit 249, and the injury to the thigh bone is Prosecutor's Exhibit 250.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, was there any evidence that suggested that these individuals had suffered injury other than gunshot injury before death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as in Kozluk, there were fractures of ribs, which could well have been crushing injuries in the grave with bodies being moved about. There were other fractures of the face and some of the other bones, which could well have been from blows from a weapon or kicking. But as I explained yesterday, it's always difficult to prove these, but that possibility certainly does exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just place page 16, which is, I think, the summary of your findings, onto the ELMO. If you could just slowly read those into the transcript, I would be grateful, and any other comments you have to add on those findings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The screen is not on. My screen is not on, so -- it's just easier to read than stretching over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a summary of the findings from the Nova Kasaba site. The site had four graves, individual graves, containing a total of 55 bodies and body parts. Most of them were in just two graves. The victims were all male, and they ranged in age from 13 to 85, or potentially from 13 to 85. There were gunshot injuries in 87 per cent of the bodies, with the average number of shots per person being 2.7. The highest proportion of the shots was to the trunk, with the head and legs next. Two people had bandaged wounds, suggestive of gunshot injuries suffered some time before. And there was evidence of shotgun pellets in five bodies, possibly from a gun discharged into the grave after death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If you could now turn to page 17 of your report, which concerns the bodies recovered from the sites at Konjevic Polje. How many bodies were presented to you and your colleagues for examination from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a much smaller grave site than the other two. This had only 12 bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, what kind of people were these in life?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These -- the age range appeared to be from about 15 to 65, and out of the whole season, we had one female victim here. All the rest appeared to be male, but there's one very definite female victim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one matter of interest, if you could place the next exhibit onto the ELMO. Could you explain to the Judges, sir, what this represents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Better that way. This is a makeshift stretcher, one of a number which were found in the grave, and it's just pieces of wood, branches, with blankets tied between them. This very much suggested that it had been used to carry either wounded people or dead bodies and, presumably, had then been put into the grave, tossed into the grave, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the most significant injury amongst all of the bodies that you observed from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these people had been shot, and the commonest site where they were shot was the trunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon had been used?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These all appeared to be a high-velocity rifle weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Place Exhibit 252 onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very typical gunshot injury to the head just above and behind the right ear. So the front of the skull here, and the ear is round about here. And here is a very typical entrance bullet hole, again with the fracturing going all over the skull.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated a moment ago in your evidence that there was a case of a female, a female body found in this grave. Can you describe to the Judges your findings in respect of that body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an interesting case in many ways, and it's a good example of the difficulties we had in establishing cause of death in some people. This was a woman who we estimated was aged anywhere between 16 and 30, and she had been shot twice in the left leg. One of these was through the hip. This is the left femur [indicates], this is the part that joins onto the pelvis [indicates], and you can see how the bone here is shattered and a bullet has gone through that. So she had been shot once in the left hip and once just below the knee. We could not prove any other injuries to her body, let alone any other gunshot injuries. There was two fractured ribs, but they didn't appear to be typical of gunshot injuries. And while gunshot injuries to the leg would be very disabling, they would not necessarily be immediately fatal, so this was an example of the situation in which we were uncertain as to -- if that was the exact cause of her death. It may have been that she was disabled, certainly, with these injuries, but died in some other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that she was placed alive and injured into the grave and suffocated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's entirely possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If you could place page 19 of your report onto the ELMO, which neatly describes your summary findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the record, the last exhibit that the witness was referring to is Prosecutor's Exhibit 253.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a small site of two graves some distance apart, between them containing 12 bodies. One person from grave 1 was female, the only one from any of the sites, and that's including Kozluk and the other sites we're discussing. There were gunshots in everyone, with three being the average number of shots to them. Most injuries were to the trunk, followed by the legs and the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If you could move to page 20 of your report, which concerns the bodies recovered from the Glogova site. How many bodies and body parts were presented to you and your colleagues from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had 90 bodies and an additional 154 body parts. This was felt by the anthropologists to give a minimum number of individuals of 147, although I'm just taking this initially from the report. They may well have a slightly more accurate figure now; I don't know. But it must be around about that, that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kinds of people were they in life?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were again apparently a relatively healthy population. Nobody had any disabilities or physical deformities. A wide age range again, potentially from 12 to 71, although one grave in particular, GL-05, had a preponderance of young people, with 46 per cent of the bodies there under the age of 24. All were male, as far as we could tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you state in your report, and indeed the Judges have already heard, that these sites or at least some of them had been extensively robbed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that affect your work at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It meant that bodies had been disturbed and parts had been disrupted, parts missing almost certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the most preponderant cause of death of the bodies that were examined by you and your colleagues from this site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, gunshot injuries was the commonest cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: High-velocity rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the majority of these individuals shot, what part of their body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it varied. The largest proportion was to the trunk. Over 50 per cent of the victims had gunshot injuries to the trunk. Next commonest was the head, and then the legs and the arms. There was one particular pattern that emerged from the graves, and this again was GL-05. This was the grave with the preponderance of young men in it. There was a very typical pattern of injury in these people of a gunshot injury to the back, to the middle of the spine. Sometimes -- in a lot of cases that have the only injury. In other -- some of the victims there were additional shots perhaps to the head, but this was a very repetitive injury and a constant finding of shattered bones in the middle of the spine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you stated, in respect of GL-05, in your evidence, that this was a younger population. I wonder if you could place Exhibit 254 on the ELMO and explain to the Judges how you concluded this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very much with the aid of the anthropologists, of course. This is a very good example. This is an upper arm bone. This is the top of the bone which goes into the shoulder. And quite apart from a injury at the lower end, if we ignore that, this is the important part here. It shows that the very top of the bone is not completely joined to the bit just below it. And this is a sign of a young person, probably somebody no older than 17. So the person is still growing. After about this age, these two parts were joined together. So the fact that they are still separate indicates that this is a young person. And this was a common finding in many of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Dr. Clark was referring to the extreme left-hand side of the photograph and the bone represented on that Exhibit, on Prosecutor's Exhibit 254.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said also in your evidence, Dr. Clark, that a very common injury that you found was a gunshot injury from the back to the spine. I think there are a number of photographs that demonstrate this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The easiest way to show this is probably that way. This is the -- I wonder if the camera would come out, if it panned out a bit. Essentially, what we're showing here is the spine coming down here, and this is the other part here. And in the middle of it here are at least two bones of the spine in small pieces, completely shattered. And the ribs on either side, they're also partly broken as well. So this area here. Imagine this is the spine going down here, and it is shattered in the middle of it. I have -- this is typical of another case, one of the bones in the spine, and this is part of the damage here. The spine is a very sturdy bone so it takes a lot of energy to fracture these bones, but this is part of the disruption here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, are these photographs and your findings consistent with individuals being shot at from behind at fairly close range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think finally in this grave, the bodies that were recovered that you and your colleagues examined, you found evidence of other forms of injury than gunshot injury, and I think there are two photographs that represent this quite well. That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 257 and 258, and if you could place 257 onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps just before we do that, just to say that there were a number of fractures of the skull and some of the long bones, that's the legs and the arm bones, which suggested perhaps kicking, stamping, or blows from a heavy weapon. In addition to that, there were two cases with very interesting injuries. These were injuries in the skull. You can see the face here, and you have this almost rectangular defect or hole in the side of the skull which is not typical of gunshot injury and is much more suggestive of something with that relative shape penetrating into the skull. An even better example, perhaps, is this case here, which shows a clear defect in the top of the skull. He had another one at the back on the -- I think it was the left side of the skull. So there were two like that. And that suggested very much to me that some pointed object like a very firm blade, perhaps, or an end of a crowbar or something of that shape had been pushed into the skull. In these two -- well, this individual particularly, there were no other injuries to account for his death, no gunshot injuries anywhere, and one has to suggest that this was probably the cause of death, whatever caused these injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And for the sake of the record, Dr. Clark referred, first of all, to Exhibit 258 and then to Exhibit 257.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, if you could just place your summary findings on the bodies and body parts recovered and presented to you from Glogova, and again add any comments that might assist the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was just one other injury type that we haven't really mentioned, and that is that a number of these bodies had clearly been burned. There was burning injury on both the clothing and on the bones themselves. Almost certainly this occurred after death, but it was a clear indication. It was also very -- concentrated very much in GL-05. This is the same grave site as the young men -- as the young man who had been shot in the spine. These were the ones showing the burning injuries. This is the summary of the finding from the Glogova site. It was a large complex site comprising a number of separate graves, five of which were exhumed this season, that's 1999. There were a total of 90 bodies and 154 body parts. All the victims were male and many of them were young, especially from the GL-05 grave. Most had been shot either once or twice, most often in the trunk, and next most commonly in the head. In GL-05, a distinct pattern of shots to the middle of the back shattering the spine with or without shots elsewhere was found. In one person, this person did not die from a gunshot injury but probably from some pointed object penetrating the skull. And there was evidence of presumed post-mortem burning of many of the bodies in GL-05 and a few in GL-02, mostly the clothing but several cases involving the bones themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Clark, it has been raised by the Defence with a number of other witnesses as to whether or not these individuals were the victims of combat or some other cause such as summary execution, and bearing in mind the limitations that you've already stated about pathology evidence in this kind of case, could you indicate to the Judges those factors which in your viewpoint against these individuals having suffered these injuries as a result of combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly nothing to suggest that these were combat casualties. It is not something that I could refute entirely, but one -- in accepting that, one would have to bear in mind various observations about these bodies. As has been said repeatedly already, there's the question of the blindfolds and ligatures on these bodies, which would be hardly findings in combat casualties. Just to repeat, in one of the graves, 41 per cent had their hands tied behind their back; 13 per cent had blindfolds around their heads, and this was also the grave; and at least 5 per cent of these people had significant physical disabilities. I think other observations we could make is that all the injuries on the bodies were bullet injuries, and there was no evidence of injuries from any other type of weapon like shrapnel or any other military weapon. Now, from the literature, it is observed frequently that the commonest type of injury in battle casualties are shrapnel injuries and bombs and other projectiles and bullets are only the second most common. This has been shown repeatedly from various studies. So just to repeat, all these injuries were bullet injuries. Also, the average number of times that these people had been shot was only 2.4, between two and three times. Now, that, I would suggest, is a fairly low average number of injuries for battle casualties, and studies have shown -- a recent study in the Gulf War, in fact, showed that the average number of injuries was nine to any one individual person. Also, in about half the victims, we could say that -- we could determine the direction of the shot, of the direction of fire, and of these, half the cases, 77 per cent had been shot in the back of the body or the side of the body and only 23 per cent had shots to the front of the body. Again, I would have thought these strong facts against these being battle casualties. Further, in at least -- in no less than ten per cent of cases, the only injury in the body was a single gunshot wound to the head, and usually to the back of the head. I think the final observation to make is that in all studies of recent conflicts, it's very obvious that far more people are wounded in combat situations than are killed, and on average, at least -- there are at least twice as many people wounded rather than killed. And to my knowledge, there's no suggestion of large numbers of wounded casualties from this area. Given the number of bodies that we found in the grave -- well, in the graves, that's almost 500 over this season, we would be expecting reports of a thousand more casualties, which to my knowledge is not the case. So all these factors, I think, go very much against this being -- these being people who were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, one clarification. There's actually a mistake in the transcript. Am I right in saying that in those cases where you could determine the direction of fire, that 77 per cent had been shot in the back or the side of the body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 23 per cent had been shot to the front of the body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you have anything further to add?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Mr. President, I can now offer the witness for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Dr. Clark, you are now going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Visnjic, I think it is. Mr. Visnjic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Clark. Dr. Clark, during your examination-in-chief, you explained to us the process of post-mortem procedure. Could you tell us the dynamics of that procedure; that is to say, how much work your team did in the course of a day, for example? How many post-mortem findings did your team have in the course of a day, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The average number -- we had at any one time three pathologists in the mortuary. The average number of cases for each pathologist per day was between three and four. So we were seeing perhaps 10 to 12 cases each day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday, you said that you took parts of the body for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which parts did you usually select for this DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually used, where available, the middle part of the right thigh bone and, if available, a tooth from each individual. These were carefully taken under as clean circumstances as we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In explaining bone injuries, you said that there were consultations between pathologists and anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which opinion was the dominant one, which one prevailed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pathologist. It was his responsibility for the final report, and it was his opinion which prevailed. I have to say there was never usually much conflict between the opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any member of your team in charge of the further identification of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the sense that we -- our scenes-of-crime officers, they looked in detail at any documents or any other artefacts taken from the body, which may have assisted further with identification. But we, as pathologists, did no more specific than what has already been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the overall conditions under which you worked and the level of preservation of the bodies that you did the post-mortems on, were you able to analyse the positions, possible positions, between the victims and their attackers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other than determining the direction of the wounds in the body, which we've already discussed. That was not possible in every case, obviously, but in a substantial number of cases we could tell these people had been shot from behind, or the front, or the side. We could not tell distance, for instance, how far away the person was when they were shot, but we could tell the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this connection, I think that my learned colleague Mr. Cayley asked you something. He asked you about a conclusion that with individuals in the grave, there were 0,5 -- I don't remember the percentage. About 70 per cent were hit from the back, and I think that the question was whether that was at a close distance or not. Were you able to determine distance in cases of that kind?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your findings in the report, you say that one of the elements to ascertain the type of injury, that you use logic, common sense. On page 3 of your report, I believe, in paragraph 5, you go on to give us some exceptions. It is the last paragraph with respect to the identification of injuries and wounds, the recognition of the injuries. Can you tell us some of those exceptions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've covered that in the paragraph 3 on the next page. This was where we found intact bullets in a body, completely undamaged bullets in a body. Now, normally with high-velocity rifle ammunition, it will pass right through the body if it doesn't strike bone. It will just go straight through the soft tissue and out through the other side. So if we found an intact bullet in the body, that indicated that it had obviously entered the body and greatly reduced speed. And possibly the most likely cause of that would be that it had already passed through someone else before striking that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in connection with that, could you tell us perhaps -- give us your opinion as to how many individuals could have been hit after being placed in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on that observation, I would have thought no more than a dozen, because it doesn't need to have been necessarily somebody else that the bullet had gone through to lose its energy. It could have been some other object. But whatever, it had clearly, by the time it entered the victim's body, had lost a lot of energy and didn't have enough energy to get out the other side, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one of the conclusions be, for example, that the body was at a greater distance from the bullet and that that might be the reason for losing the high velocity? When I say "at a distance", I'm thinking about, say, several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have to be a long distance, because these bullets have high velocity over a long distance. I don't know the exact figures, but I would have thought certainly more than 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 of your report -- that is to say, my question is the following: In principle, should you state the causes of death in cases where many parts of the body are missing? What is your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a part on the body -- even though large parts are missing, if there's an obviously fatal injury in that body, I think it would be quite justified in saying that was the cause of death. For instance, if all we had was the upper half of a body with the skull and the trunk, but both legs were missing, if there's a gunshot wound in the skull, that's necessarily and inevitably fatal. So it doesn't matter that the rest of the body is missing. That is the fatal injury. The reverse does not apply, however. If all we found was a gunshot injury to the leg and the skull was missing, we would not accept that as the cause of death. But bullet wounds to certain parts of the body, I think one can assume that that's going to be a fatal injury.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the part of your report which speaks about post-mortems in Kozluk, you state that the degree of preservation of the body in the grave -- that is to say, that the preservation of the bodies was different, the degree of that and the degree of decomposition, and you mention several reasons for that. Could one of the reasons be the fact that some bodies were exposed for longer periods of time to the elements, in comparison to the other bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could one of the reasons be the fact that some bodies were buried straight away on the spot, whereas others could have been brought from elsewhere and buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a possibility, if we're speaking about a substantial time period, a time period such that the bodies could -- the decomposition process could develop quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the section on Kozluk in your report, and with the other graves as well, you make a table giving the numbers of shots per body, per person.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the state of the bodies during the post-mortems, the number of shots that you mention, is that the least number of possible shots per person?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the shots that we were very sure that this was a gunshot injury. There were other injuries on these bodies which could have been gunshot injuries, but we were not 100 per cent convinced they were, so we didn't count these. So, yes, these are minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also possible that the projectile passed through the soft tissues without injuring the bone and that is why you did not record that particular injury, because the soft tissues had disintegrated, become decomposed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your experience, how often is the likelihood of this happening?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are bones in most parts of the body. The one part of the body which injuries could be reflected without leaving any bony injury would be the abdomen. So we may well have missed some abdominal injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This possibility exists if the body is not complete, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you also state that in certain cases, some pathologists considered the cause of death to be undetermined, whereas others, for the same description, thought that the description was sufficient to determine the cause of death. I suppose that that is due to different standards applied.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was mostly for people who had been shot perhaps in the legs. Some people felt that a gunshot injury to, say the thigh, would necessarily have caused damage to blood vessels and could well have been fatal. Others were a little more cautious and said, "Well, that's not" -- they weren't entirely happy with that, and we just had to go along with that. I think the numbers we're speaking about here are fairly small in that respect, but I think everyone accepted that a gunshot injury to the head, any sign of a gunshot injury to the chest or the trunk or the pelvis was certainly a potentially fatal injury, and it was only with the limb injuries when we had some debate about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When determining the cause of death, on page 10 you explained -- this is about Kozluk -- that in 55 cases, it was not possible to establish the cause of death, 55 per cent of the cases, and -- no, 55 cases. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The problem was in the translation. Fifty-five cases. And you also included the possibility of other causes as well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible, on the basis of traces on the sublingual bone, to establish knife injuries in the area of the neck?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the term "sublingual bone," but I presume you're meaning the bones of the throat, the thyroid cartridge and the hyoid bone probably. Yes, I understand your question. Yes. These are bones which don't -- because these are very fragile bones, these are bones that don't preserve well, and in the majority of people they were no longer present. It is possible, if people had had their throats cut, that you could injure these bones but certainly by no means invariably. So I wouldn't count it as -- the absence or presence of injuries to the bones I wouldn't count as a great indicator of such injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: In view of the global impression that you have about the graves, would you allow for the possibility that some bodies were brought from the outside, from different locations, and buried in individual graves subsequently? In individual cases, could that be a possibility or do you exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exclude that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, you said that you conducted post-mortems on 292 bodies. On the other hand, Professor Wright, in his report on exhumations in Kozluk in 1999, on page 12, says that 291 bodies were exhumed. Is there an explanation for the difference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could be. One possibility is that we, in the mortuary -- because we had 292 bodies and we also had a large number of body parts. Now, sometimes, and this was particularly in some of the later graves, what the anthropologists liked to call a body part, we felt more comfortable, having seen the body laid out and cleaned up, to call it a body because it had all the significant parts present, and I imagine that's what the discrepancy is there. I think you will certainly find that in the Glogova site where we changed from bodies to body parts quite a lot, but that was because, in the mortuary, we felt we had all the evidence there, and it was a judgement whether to call this a full body in the sense that all the major parts were there as opposed to a body part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to go on to the part of your report dealing with the grave at Nova Kasaba. On page 14 of your report, the section dealing with the distribution of shots and injury patterns, we find that there were 33 shots to the head of the victim. You also state, on the same page, in the section dealing with the direction of shots and distance fired, that it was not possible to determine the direction. In view of the fact that these were injuries to the head, is it possible that if they were inflicted at close range, these injuries, that there would be traces on the bones of explosions, gunpowder explosions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been minute traces. Most of the evidence on establishing distance of fire requires the skin and soft tissues, because that is where the gunpowder and other deposits and the burning are deposited. There may well be minute traces which get into the bone themselves, but we certainly did not look for them. I think it would be extraordinarily difficult to do that and there was no clear evidence of that. I feel the absence does not exclude the possibility of close firing. As I say, the bulk of the evidence for that, close firing, is on the skin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this particular case, that is, the Nova Kasaba grave, are there any traces confirming close-range fire, any evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no positive evidence of it and there's no negative evidence. In other words, we cannot tell definitely one way or the other but it's not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the time, I don't know whether it would be convenient to have a break now. Should I continue with my cross?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need more or less?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think then it is better to have a break now. So we're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are resuming the hearing. Mr. Visnjic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in the response you gave regarding the coordination of views among the individual pathologists regarding the cause of death, you said that some discussion occurred defining injuries to the thigh area. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just the thigh -- I just used that as an example -- but we discussed the findings between us as would happen in any professional situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a person was injured in the thigh with a bullet from a firearm with large destructive power and from a relatively close range of a few metres perhaps, and the nervous sciatic was damaged in the process, in your opinion would that person's life be in danger? Would it be fatal, in other words?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would not be necessarily immediately fatal. In fact, it wouldn't be immediately fatal. The person would be disabled. They certainly wouldn't be able to walk. They would start losing blood. But it is a treatable condition if emergency first aid is given to try and bandage these wounds. If the person was left with a large gaping injury to the thigh and given no medical assistance, then eventually, I think, they probably would have died. But we're speaking hours, if not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That person, what are the possibilities for that person to move about without assistance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can never underestimate what people can do in situations, and they potentially could crawl or heave themselves around. Yes, that's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could that person cover a certain distance, a kilometre, or several hundred metres, or maybe more, if you can give us an answer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's almost impossible to answer these questions. I would say nothing is impossible, and a person with the will power and the strength of will to do that could probably do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question has to do with the Glogova grave. On page 21, you describe the number of shots on the bodies. In accordance with your previous answer, I assume that in this case too, these are the minimum number of shots per person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have seen Exhibits 257, 258, that is, two skulls, Prosecution exhibits, on which injuries are shown inflicted by a blow with a blunt object. Could it be established whether these injuries were inflicted post-mortem or ante-mortem?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for definite this was ante-mortem or post-mortem, just as with the gunshot injuries. All I can say is that these were the only injuries on this person, and that must raise the possibility that these happened in life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the possibility of them being inflicted post-mortem is not excluded, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not excluded. I'm not sure how it would be inflicted, but I can't exclude that these are post-mortem injuries, no, particularly bearing in mind that there are two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this grave, that is, Glogova, were there several burials, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there appeared to be several different graves within the overall grave site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in answer to a question by my learned friend Mr. Cayley, you spoke about your overall impression regarding the causes of death in all the grave sites on the basis of your investigations in 1999. If we exclude Nova Kasaba grave site, Konjevic Polje, and perhaps a part of the grave site in Glogova, is there a greater probability that the persons buried in those graves did not meet their death as a consequence of mass executions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is fair to say, because one of the pointers against all of these people, that is, all the four grave sites being combat casualties was the fact that in Kozluk, at least, so many had blindfolds and ligatures and disabilities. So in that sense, the fact that Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, and Glogova, none of the victims there had blindfolds or ligatures, none of them had any obvious physical disabilities, yes, that does reduce the pointers against, but still doesn't take away from the fact that there were no injuries from other military weapons. And I stress that in combat situations, the commonest type of injury are injuries other than bullets; in other words, fragmenting items such as grenades and shells. And this has been shown repeatedly in many conflicts, not least in Croatia in 1992. Also, we still have the evidence that the bulk of people had been shot to the back of the body rather than the front, and the absence of the large numbers of wounded which we would expect in a combat situation. But to return to your overall initial question, yes, excluding Kozluk, the pointers against the other three grave sites being combat casualties are reduced. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That ends my cross-examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Cayley, some additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I just have a few questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Cayley:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, could you find in the pile of photographs Exhibits 248, 252, and 256. Actually, if you could place 252 onto the ELMO first. Dr. Clark, this is a skull that we've already discussed, and it's from the Konjevic Polje site. That's where the body was recovered from. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the bullet to the side of the head is a fairly well-aimed shot if one was intending to kill this individual?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the immediate assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could then place Exhibit 248 onto the ELMO. This is from another grave. This is Nova Kasaba. Again, considering the shot to the middle of the back of the head, if you were intending to kill this person, would this be a fairly well-aimed shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we had a large number of people in which this was a very typical injury, an injury -- a bullet hole to the back either in the midline or just to the side of it. This was a very common finding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could finally turn to Exhibit 256, which is from Glogova, and this is, I think, a shot to the middle of the spine from the back, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Better like that. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, stating the obvious, if you were intending to kill somebody, this is a place where you would shoot them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. I mean, it's a shot to the middle of the back. It's not an area which would be immediately fatal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it could be fatal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be fatal, yes, but it's not as immediately fatal as a shot to the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, considering these three photographs, and we spoke about distance, the distance from which somebody could have fired to actually hit these three individuals, I know you've stated that in order to determine distance accurately, you need to be able to inspect soft tissue, but would you agree with me that these three photographs at least provide a factor that would suggest that they were fired at from close range because of the position that these bullets hit these bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree entirely. They are, if you like, targeted areas, and it is easier to target somewhere the closer you are to the person, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doctor, not professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are a senior lecturer.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In my country they would call you Professor. Now, just one question and then -- two questions perhaps. The first one is a minor one. You might be able to tell me about it. You said that in Glogova site, they each started at 12 and from 12 to 71. What was the percentage of the children? Twelve is children, I mean, between 12 and 18, for instance. Could you tell me what was the percentage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I'm going to be a little hesitant of giving ages. This is more the anthropologists who determine this. What I can say is from their reports they gave us ranges, and they ranged from as young as 12. That's not to say that we had a 12-year-old, but within the limits of being able to determine these things, it could have been as young as that. I don't know -- all I do know is that in GL-05, there was a preponderance of young people. I think we're speaking about people in their late teens, early 20s mainly, rather than 12- or 13-year-old children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In their teens?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, late teens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Late teens would be 16 or 17?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's a teenager.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, late teens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But if they couldn't decide if they were 12 or 13, how could they decide that they had people at the age of 85? Is it easier to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's easier to age people the younger they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's easier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How could they age that people were 85?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a sort of broad range they've given. I mean after the age of about 45 or 50, it's actually very difficult to age them at all, and this was just an upper range they gave. I mean, I suppose they could have said a hundred, but there's no real cutoff point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But definitely it was old age?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people who could have been older, yes. The trouble is after about the age of 40 or 50, it's almost impossible, just from looking at the bones, to say that that person was 50 or was 60 or was 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: After the age of 50 or 40?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly that, yes. Forty, mid-40s to 50, it becomes increasingly difficult to tie down an age even within about 10 or 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you mentioned -- just another little question -- most shots or injuries were from gunshots, and you said it was, for instance, 87 per cent in Nova Kasaba. What was the source of the other injuries in such cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 87 per cent, I suspect, is an underestimate. That was the number of gunshots which we professionally felt we could definitely prove. There were other injuries on these bodies which could well have been gunshot injuries, but in the limits of our proof, we could not say definitely they were. Other people could have died from blunt-force injuries, kicking injuries, beating injuries; that's a possibility. There were a number of individuals in which we actually found no injuries whatsoever on the body, no fractures, no nothing, and that included some bodies which were well preserved. They could have died in other ways, including natural cause. They may have been elderly people who had travelled some distance, maybe had heart conditions, and who just collapsed in the heat or whatever. I suspect that there will be a few people like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now I come to my main question, and perhaps it's due to a difference between your scientific approach and the social science approach. In the social science approach, there is always room for doubt, but sometimes in the scientific approach you are more categorical. So I would like to understand more your answer concerning the possibility that the injuries resulted from a fight or battle injuries. First, in your answer to the Prosecutor, you said that you cannot refute entirely that these injuries resulted from combat, but you mentioned many reasons, which you repeated to the Defence counsel, and I noted them down, of course, that hand tied; physical disabilities; people were shot in the back; and people were usually wounded in a fight and not only all killed; of course the back shots too; and many, many other reasons which you mentioned, and then still you said that you cannot refute entirely. Is there any reason to doubt that this could result from fight? You said that perhaps concerning Kozluk. You seem to have excluded Kozluk. You said that there are pointers, reduced pointers to the contrary with regard to Kozluk. Speaking of Kozluk, you mentioned that 41 per cent had their hands ligated, that 13 per cent were blindfolded, that some were shot seven times, and most in the head. Now, why did you exclude Kozluk from your general assessment that it was not -- that these injuries could not be battle injuries? Was Kozluk, in your opinion, a fight?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be fair, I was asked to exclude Kozluk by the Defence, and that was a rather separate grave because that was the only grave with the people with ligatures and blindfolds. And I would have thought that's a very, very strong pointer against these being combat casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the others?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others are less, because we don't have that factor. I see what -- you're trying to say, "Why is there any doubt?" Well, it depends what you mean by "combat casualties", and it's up to others to put that forward. But we have people who have been shot. Now, this is two groups of men facing each other or fighting each other. It is still possible that in that situation, a number could be shot in the back, if there was surprise from a different direction. If it's a situation that the only weapons being used in that -- unusually being used in that situation were guns, then that still leaves a possibility. So it very much depends on what sort of combat is being presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in the other sites, there is a possibility there could have been a combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't entirely exclude it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You can't entirely?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But, for instance, for --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm saying the findings would be very untypical from all the other findings from other conflicts reported in the literature, and this is in context with the type of injuries which have been inflicted, the lack of wounded individuals and, to some extent, the direction of shots. I think these are very strong pointers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They are strong pointers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But only in Kozluk, it was --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozluk is even more strong, because it's inconceivable that you could suggest that people were fighting with their hands tied behind their backs or fighting with blindfolds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there any people with hands tied behind their backs in the other sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the other pointers were there; shots in the back?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the other pointers were certainly there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were certainly there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madame Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I have just one question. In your summaries of the various sites from which you examined bodies, you pointed out -- in a few cases, you pointed out similarities or what might be systemic patterns in the places where the shots appeared in the bodies, et cetera. You've also pointed out the differences in the ligatures, the presence of ligatures and blindfolds in Kozluk. Would you say, looking at all the sites from which you have examined bodies, and excluding for the moment the possibility of combat, excluding the hypothesis of combat, and accepting the hypothesis which I did take to be the one that you thought more likely, that there had been mass executions of some sort at these various sites, would you say that your observations of the patterns of injury were more consistent with all of those burials being under a unified plan or part of a general motus operandi, or would they be just as consistent with a hypothesis that you could have had four or five spontaneous killings, of executions, unconnected with each other, which resulted in the bodies that went into the different graves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different patterns between some of the graves, and I would suspect that this was different -- these were different incidents, albeit carried out in the same general intention. But we did have some slightly different patterns. I was mentioning the very distinctive pattern in Glogova, the shots in the back. Some of the grave sites, the average number of shots was higher than others, so that there were subtle differences between some of the grave sites -- between the grave sites, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And your general -- just to follow through on that, your general knowledge and observations of mass graves or the results of executions here and in the past would have led you to tilt in which direction; that these grave sites were basically part of a single operation or they just as consistently could have come about from spontaneous reactions in different places?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can distinguish the two, if the two should necessarily be distinguished. If you're saying this is the same person or group of persons going around and killing all of these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Not the same persons, perhaps, but some general pattern, command operation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that we have what appeared to be deliberately targeted injuries in each of these grave sites, yes, there is an overall pattern of execution-type injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Dr. Clark, I shall perhaps go a little further but along the same path as my colleagues. Your experience has allowed you to reconstruct the situation that occurred before what you actually observed, and you were asked, when doing these post-mortems, in a sense to reconstruct the situation prior to death. Are you in a position to give us a general idea, after having observed a large number of bodies and body parts, are you in a position to give us a general idea of what you were able to reconstruct, the situation that led up to these consequences that you actually observed? I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a difficult question. Our main -- my main expertise was in looking at the bodies. I think you've got to take into consideration the findings at the grave sites and how bodies were placed in the graves, which I don't have any detailed knowledge of. All I would say is that from the findings of the bodies overall, there's every indication that these were people who were executed and placed in the various graves. I don't think I can go much farther than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Cayley, I think we have some documents to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. We do. The first exhibit is Prosecution Exhibit 195, which is a document that shows the sites which Dr. Clark was concerned with; Exhibit 235, which is his curriculum vitae; Exhibit 236, which is his report; 236A, which is the B/C/S version of that report; 237, which is the example of the autopsy report, and 238, which is the table of nationalities of his staff. 239 to 257 are the photographs. If I could apply for formal admission of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, have you any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the exhibits are admitted into evidence as a whole. You may be seated, Mr. Cayley. Dr. Clark, you have finished your testimony and your communication with us here. We wish to thank you very much for coming here, and we also thank you for the work you have done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the next witness, there's a small housekeeping matter, and it concerns the evidence of Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez. Mr. Ruez testified on the 15th of March of this year in respect of an exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 22/8. This is on page 742 of the transcript. He stated that that photograph was taken in April of 1998, and he was mistaken. The Prosecutor's records indicate that that photograph was, in fact, taken on the 21st of April, 1997. My learned friend Mr. Harmon has spoken with the Defence on this matter. They are in agreement to stipulate to that fact in order to correct the transcript, and I bring it to the Court's attention so that it can be placed on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have discussed this matter with representatives of the Prosecution, and after the evidence provided, we agreed that this was indeed an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Madam Registrar, will you please take note of this and make the correction in the transcript along the lines proposed by Mr. Cayley. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is going to be taken by the senior trial attorney, so I will retire to the back and allow him to come forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Lawrence. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration that the usher has handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you are quite familiar with the proceedings in a courtroom, so you will feel quite at ease. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Lawrence, you will first be answering questions put to you by Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President, counsel. Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, because we speak the same language, I'm going to ask you to pause after I finish my question so the interpreters have time to catch up with the final interpretation of the question, and I'll pause after you give an answer so they can do the same.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, Dr. Lawrence, could you state your full name and can you spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Christopher Hamilton Lawrence. Lawrence is spelled L-a-w-r-e-n-c-e.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current occupation, Dr. Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist employed at the New South Wales Institute of Forensic Medicine in Sydney Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours and counsel should have a copy of the curriculum vitae of Dr. Lawrence. It's marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 221.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just take you through some of the salient portions of this CV, Dr. Lawrence. First of all, what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I am Australian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber of your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I have a medical degree from the University of Sydney, where I graduated in 1983. That is the American equivalent of the MD. I have a science degree in physiology also from the University of Sydney. I am a fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Pathologists, which as a pathologist, it is the American equivalent of the board certification in pathology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me focus on your education. When you received your Bachelor of Medical Science in physiology, did you receive any prizes or medals?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I was the winner of the P.O. Bishop Medal and the H.G. Chapman prize for that thesis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- can you explain those prizes and why they were awarded?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: They were awarded to the top Bachelor of Medical Science graduate of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn briefly to some other aspects of your career. Between October 1989 and June of 1991 were you appointed as a specialist in forensic medicine in New South Wales, to the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Glebe, Australia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between June of 1991 and June 1993, were you a Fellow in forensic pathology in the State of New Mexico in the United States at the Office of the Medical Examiner at the University of New Mexico School of Medicine in Albuquerque?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In the first year, I was a Fellow. In the second year I acted as a staff pathologist at the Office of the Medical Investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from August of 1994 until the present time, have you been appointed and do you act as a clinical lecturer at the Department of Pathology at the University of Sydney in Australia?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to those qualifications, Dr. Lawrence, have you been accepted as an expert in the field of forensic pathology in the courts of your country?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you been accepted as an expert in the field of forensic pathology in courts in the United States?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I have been accepted -- sorry. Yes, I have been accepted as an expert witness in the States of New Mexico and Colorado.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, we've heard, in the last few days, testimony about the composition of exhumation teams that examined human remains in Bosnia at various times and the interrelationship between anthropologist and pathologist. I don't intend to ask you a great deal about anthropology, but have you had some training in anthropology?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Yes, I have had training in forensic anthropology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe just the extent of that training?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In addition to practical experience, I have attended a number of courses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were those courses?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I attended courses at the Smithsonian Institute in Washington, the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology course which was run in New Mexico, another forensic anthropology course run in New Mexico, and a course run in the investigation of buried remains in Brisbane.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Lawrence. Now, what was your role in exhumations conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor in Bosnia in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I was the -- sorry. I was the chief pathologist in Bosnia for the ICTY in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit 259 placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps that is in front of you, Dr. Lawrence. If not, the usher will assist you. It is this exhibit. Now, Dr. Lawrence, how many sites were exhumed in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Eight sites.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your responsibility to examine the human remains from each of those exhumed sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, does the Prosecutor's exhibit which has been placed on the ELMO identify in orange the sites from which you examined human remains?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard testimony earlier in this case, Dr. Lawrence, but for the sake of clarity for the people in the gallery, only one of the sites that you exhumed was a primary grave site?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the sites was a robbed primary site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all of the -- and that is the site that is indicated as the dam; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other locations marked on this exhibit in orange were secondary grave sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you examined the human remains from each of those sites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "you," I mean you and members of your staff.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, in respect of each of these sites that are marked in orange, was a report prepared by you in respect of the findings made at each of those sites?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in front of you, Dr. Lawrence, are the reports that were prepared by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, that includes Prosecutor's Exhibit 261, which is the primary site of the dam; 262, which is the secondary site CR-12; a report on autopsies at 263 dealing with Cancari Road 3; 264 dealing with autopsies for the Hodzici Road site 3; 265, Hodzici Road site 4; 266, which deals with the findings in respect of Hodzici Road 5; 267, which is Zeleni Jadar site 5; and lastly, 268, which is the Liplje site 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark -- Dr. Lawrence, I'm sorry, in addition to those reports that deal with sites that were exhumed and your analysis of the human remains from those sites, did you also prepare a report in respect of human remains found on the surface at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. There were two body parts recovered in 1998, and those were examined because it was felt incorrect to leave them till the next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that, for the record, the report prepared by Dr. Lawrence is a one-page report. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 260.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, we've heard about the procedures that were used by Dr. Clark and his team that assisted him in respect of the exhumations in 1999. You operated in Bosnia in 1998, and I'd like to focus then on your procedures on what facilities were available to you. Could you, first of all, describe to the Trial Chamber the morgue facility that was available to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. The morgue facility used was the same one as was used in 1999. It is the Gradska Groblja mortuary facility in Visoko. It had three tables; it had facilities for fluoroscopic equipment, and a secure room where evidence could be locked. During the course of the year, we had more material than we could conveniently handle in that facility, and for the last third of the year, we also used two temporary mortuaries which were also on the site which also had another three or four tables in them in order to facilitate the processing of the remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
