utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, in order to convey succinctly the procedures that you used in 1998 that were followed by members of your staff, I'd like to take you through a case study, if you will, and what I'd like you to do is describe the procedures that were used by you and members of your staff upon receipt of a body bag containing human remains and take us through the procedure to the time the analysis and the examination had been completed, the body bag was sewn up and turned over to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. The body bags were received in a locked, refrigerated container. I had one key. The crime-scene officer from the scene had one key. We removed the bodies from the refrigerated container as we were using them and locked it after we had taken the bodies out. The bodies were taken out, and as soon as the body bags were opened, a photograph was taken of the contents of the body bag. The body bag would then be taken by the pathologist who is going to handle the case and X-rayed using a portable X-ray equipment, a fluoroscope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me stop right there for a moment, Dr. Lawrence, and I'd like you to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 262, which is the report on autopsies of human remains from Cancari Road site 12. There are four photographs following page 5 of your report, and I'd like you to take each of those photographs and inform the Trial Chamber of what the procedure was when you're fluoroscoping these remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, in that report, Dr. Lawrence will be referring to the four photographs immediately after page five of his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see you've placed the first photograph on the ELMO. Why don't you describe this particular procedure.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This photograph depicts or shows an image made by the fluoroscope. It depicts the -- a left elbow joint with the joint itself in the centre of the picture. You can see a number of fractures in the bone just above centre here, and you can see a shadow here which represents a metal object which is, in fact, a bullet. Now, the pathologist would look on the fluoroscope for fractures and for bullets. If it was convenient at the time, he would recover the bullet and submit it for evidence. If not, he might wait and recover it later. He would also look for any bony abnormalities that could be demonstrated on X-ray. He would then prepare a handwritten report on what he saw, and the body would then be taken from the fluoroscope to the main area where it would be placed on a table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, would you explain the successive three photographs in this particular report. And this, I take it, depicts an injury of some kind. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. This is from the same case as the fluoroscope. It shows -- sorry. It shows the left forearm [indicates] on the right of the picture. There is a hole in the skin here and a second hole here. These correspond to bullet holes. This tissue [indicates] has been cleaned for the purposes of examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn to the next picture, please, Dr. Lawrence. What is that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This shows [indicates] the bullet that we could see -- sorry, the bullet is slightly to the left here. This shows the bullet recovered from the soft tissue. You can see it has the same outlines as the X-ray image. This was marked and submitted for evidence. Now, finally, to confirm the presence of the gunshot wound, this is the same case again [indicates]. This is the distal or the elbow part of the left upper arm, and you can see the anthropologists have reconstructed the fractured humerus. The white material here is glue, and you can see the path where the bullet has gone through the elbow joint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Lawrence. Why don't you continue with describing the procedure. After the human remains or the body is removed from the fluoroscope room, what happens?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Once the body is removed from the fluoroscope room, it's put on the main -- on the working table. It is searched, the clothing is removed, and the external surface of the body is examined for evidence of injuries. Now, at this stage the procedure would vary depending on whether there was a large amount of soft tissue or the remains were skeletalised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, why don't we start with the procedure with the body that has a large amount of flesh remaining on it. First of all, so we're perfectly clear in what you mean by that, if you would turn to your report, Prosecution Exhibit 263, the image following page 6 of that, would you place that on the ELMO, please. What is that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is a body from Cancari 3, showing a relatively intact body with relatively complete soft tissue. What you can see at the top is the head, chest, the arms, pelvis, and the legs [indicates]. Relatively speaking for this site, this was a body with a large amount of soft tissue. Probably only around five per cent of the bodies were in as good a condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, let's proceed with your description of the procedure, with what happens when you have a fleshed body, what you do. We're going to come back later to the procedures when you have just a skeleton or skeletalised body.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The body would then be searched for items of identification, for personal items, and the clothing would be removed. The body would then be washed, and the pathologist would examine the external surfaces of the body carefully for injuries. At that stage, the clothing would be tagged with the case name and taken off. I'll come back to that in a minute. The pathologist would then carry out -- sorry. At this stage, if there were external gunshot wounds, for example, or other external obvious injuries, they would be photographed. The pathologist, assisted by the assistant, would then open the body, open the areas of injury, and attempt to define them further. Where there were still organs present, those would be examined for evidence of significant injury. In the case of bony injury, the bones would be examined. If they were severely broken, they would be removed and reconstructed in order to ascertain, as we saw with the elbow, to confirm the presence of the bullet track.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would do the reconstruction of the bone?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The reconstruction of the bone would routinely be done by the anthropologists assigned to the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the course of examining the bodies, if you found an abnormal feature, for example, an old injury or something that was unique, would you record that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. We also examined the body for evidence of identifying features. These were old injuries, malformations, deformities, evidence of tooth decay, or anything that might help later on identify the individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have an example that you can illustrate that particular point in the exhibits in front of you? I believe if you refer to Prosecutor's Exhibit 263, there may be one such illustration you could put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I have two here. The first of these, what you can see here just to the left of the centre is a grossly-deformed ulna. That is one of the two bones of the forearm. Now, you can see from the scale that it is extremely short. It is also extremely badly malformed. This person would have effectively had an extremely short and strange-looking right forearm. This would be a fairly characteristic sort of deformity and would have caused significant problems with the function of the right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your purpose in noting these kind of deformities to assist in later identification of individuals?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That was the primary purpose, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have another illustration from the same exhibit?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is the spine of one of the bodies from CR-3. What you can see is severe -- sorry -- severe sclerosis of the spine. This person effectively had a completely fused spine. This would be fairly characteristic and would have produced a large degree of incapacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other kinds of disabilities did you locate in the course of conducting medical examinations in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: We found people with evidence of old fractures of the hip that had never healed. We found old gunshot wounds with severe persistent damage to the joints. We found a man who had had a tracheostomy; that is, a tube placed in his throat. Presumably, the sort of previous tumour of the larynx, but unfortunately we couldn't tell. The significant thing about this person is that with the tracheostomy, he would be unable to speak. We found people with injuries that had been bandaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point in the procedure you've been describing, you've done the medical examination of the flesh body, where does the anthropologist fit in?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The anthropologist, in the fleshed bodies, would come in to do the reconstructions of the bones, as I described. But their other function would be to look at the pubic bones, look at the skull, look at the long bones, to try and ascertain the age and sex and the height of the individual. In addition, they had an important function, in looking at the bony injuries, to consult with the pathologist as to whether these injuries occurred at or around the time of death, i.e., that they are what's called pari-mortem injuries, or whether they were post-mortem injuries. Those are injuries that have occurred after the time of death which may have occurred during the burial, digging up, reburial, or even re-extraction of the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it the pathologist and the anthropologist would consult about their respective findings.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen then?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: After the pathologist had consulted with the anthropologist and reviewed the reconstructed bones, the pathologist would then prepare a handwritten report. He would often use diagrams to diagram the areas of injury. He would hand over the pieces of evidence that had been taken from the body to the crime scene officer. In the case of the clothing, the clothing would be taken off and washed. Once it had been washed and dried, it would be examined by one of the crime scene officers for the evidence of injury. The purpose of this was that given that many of our bodies had lost their skin, damage to the clothing was sometimes the only evidence we had that there may have been a bullet injury. The clothing was also examined for evidence of military origin and also for any characteristic identifying features. Now, the crime scene officer would then prepare a report on the clothing, indicating where he found damage. Now, in the event that the pathologist had an injury that he was not certain about, he might actually go early in the piece and examine the clothing directly in order to corroborate his injuries. Obviously, if there is a gunshot wound in the middle of the chest, then there is likely to be -- there is going to be a corresponding defect in the clothing. So the pathologist would cross-index his findings with the clothing. In any event, the pathologist, before he finished the report, would check the clothing to make sure that there were corresponding defects in the clothing to account for the gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would the clothing be tagged with a number similar to the tag number on the body itself?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: As the clothing was removed from the body, the assistant would place a tag on every item, clearly marking the case number of the item.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this report has been prepared by you, in consultation with the anthropologist, and after the clothing has been examined, what's the next step in the procedure?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: At that stage, the pathologist would check the report, sign the typewritten -- sorry. A typewritten copy would be made of the handwritten report, which would include the pathologist's opinion as to the cause of death, amongst other things, and he would check that report, check all of the evidence against it, and sign the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen to the body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The body, at the completion of the examination, would be resealed with the case number clearly written on it and would be stored for handing over to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, let's take the other situation that you described, because not all of the bodies that you were examining were fleshed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why don't you describe then, if you will, to the Chamber, the procedure that was used when you had skeletalised remains only.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: If I may show an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, and if you would refer to Prosecutor's Exhibit 261, which is the report on the dam, I believe. I think there are two examples or two photographs that you and I had discussed to show to the Trial Chamber to illustrate this particular point. They are the photographs that follow page 4, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This photograph shows the initial step in the process. This is a body bag [indicates] which has been opened as it first comes into the mortuary, showing the remains in the body bag as we first received them. Now, those would then be taken and fluoroscoped. We've discussed that. In the event of skeletal remains, after the clothing had been removed and searched and the physical evidence identified, the bones would then be initially examined before washing in order to examine the colour of the fractures. Now, I think Dr. Clark has alluded to the difficulty in trying to identify the problems between fractures that occurred at the time of death and the fractures that occurred after death. But in a certain number of cases where the fractures are fairly fresh, that is, occurred post-mortem and were reasonably close to the time of examination, examination of the edge of the bones may reveal a very clear pale colour, which may give an indication that that injury has occurred in the post-mortem period. So the bones were examined initially before washing to establish whether they were definite post-mortem injuries. Once they had been examined, they were then washed and they would be aligned in an anatomical position by the anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're turning the page and you'll show us the next exhibit in the same document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That is correct. This is, in fact, the same case, Dam-001, after it had been washed and laid in an anatomical -- roughly anatomical position. You can see at the top the two upper arm bones, the left shoulder blade, the sternum, the thoracic spine, and the ribs. The bones were cleaned up and aligned in this anatomical position in an attempt to assess whether injuries had occurred in the pari-mortem period when all of the bodies were in an anatomical position or whether they could have occurred in the post-mortem interval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen after that examination?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, the pathologist and the anthropologist would both examine these and look for evidence of injury. Some of the injuries, as you can see in this particular one, this fracturing along here is almost certainly a post-mortem injury due to weathering and damage. But the -- again, where there were fractures of bones that were -- where it was difficult to see what the actual centre of the injury looked like, they would be reconstructed. Again, the bodies would be searched for injury, for identifying features. The anthropologist would examine the remains for evidence of sex, age, and stature, and the evidence taken from the body would then be bagged. The pathologist and the anthropologist would usually consult regarding the injuries, because in these particular cases, the anthropologist had a lot of experience at looking at pure bony injury. At the end of that, the pathologist would form an opinion as to the injuries present and complete a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, you've shown us one example of an elbow being -- elbow bones being reconstructed by the anthropologist. I'd just like to illustrate that point one more time. If you would turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 263, which is your report from the Report on Autopsies of Human Remains from Cancari Road 3, and if you would put on the ELMO the illustration that follows page 9 of that report. I'd like you to, first of all, identify the exhibit and then explain it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is the photograph referred to. This is a skull from one of the bodies from Cancari Road 3. It has been -- what we can see here is the top of the skullcap, the front of the skull on the left there is a gunshot wound in the centre marked by the arrow, with a series of radiating fractures. The white represents glue used to do the reconstruction. You can also see a degree of deformity, persistent deformity of the skull in addition. You notice the area around the gunshot wound is reasonably underformed. The gunshot wound is a pari-mortem injury, but it appears, in addition, there is some crushing injury which is probably post-mortem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Dr. Lawrence, this is an example of a reconstruction of bone, in this case the skull, performed by an anthropologist, that would assist you in your examination and determination of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be quite hard to see the bullet hole until the fragments of skull were stuck back together again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Lawrence, you have prepared eight complete reports of the eight exhumation sites from which human remains were removed in 1998. I do not intend to take you through each of these reports. What I would like you to do is go through one of those reports, because the formatting in each of these reports is the same; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And using the Prosecution Exhibit 263, which is the report on autopsies of human remains from the Cancari Road site 3, I'd like you to take us through the report, and if you would start by putting on the ELMO the page 2, which is your Summary and Conclusions on Autopsies from CR-03. If you would place that on the ELMO, and if you would read your findings into the record in respect of this particular site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We're going to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, we're resuming. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, before the break I'd asked you to examine and take your report, which is the report of Autopsies on Human Remains from Cancari Road 3, and we'll go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But just so the record is perfectly clear, the site indicated as Cancari Road 3, Your Honours, has been linked to the Kozluk primary grave site, as can be seen in Prosecutor's Exhibit 259. Those links were testified to by Dean Manning, and he has identified the various sources of those links that can be seen on Prosecutor's Exhibit 259.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, Dr. Lawrence, would you place on the ELMO the Summary and Conclusions of the Autopsies from Cancari Road 3 site and just read into the record those findings, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Thank you. Summary and Conclusions on Autopsies from CR-03. 1. From the anthropological examination, the grave at CR-03 site is estimated to contain at least 160 individuals. 2. All of the bodies where sex could be determined, that's 126, were male. There was one subadult, a teenager, who wore some female clothing and was of an indeterminate sex by anthropological examination. 3. There was one individual between the ages of 8 and 13 years, a child, and at least seven over the age of 65 years. 4. None of the bodies were carrying weapons or wearing army or militia uniforms. One of the bodies appeared to be wearing a blue uniform, but this did not appear to be a police uniform or have obvious military insignia. In one of the general body bags, that is, a mixed collection of isolated bones and clothing, there was a Yugoslav National Army jacket. 5. There were 37 twine or fabric ligatures, wrist bindings; 25 of those were associated with hands or on arms, 8 were with bodies, and 4 were found loose in the graves. In four cases, the hands appeared to be secured behind the back. The material of the ligatures is similar to that seen in CR-12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you there for just a moment. Again referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 259, CR-12 is linked to Branjevo Military Farm primary execution site. With that clarification, Dr. Lawrence, please continue reading from your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: 6. Eight blindfolds were found on or around the bodies at this site. Four of these were around the face. 7. The bodies were decomposed but varied considerably from having recognisable organs to complete skeletonisation with disarticulation, that is, complete loss of soft tissue with separation of the body parts. 8. There were 225 definite gunshot wounds, five probable gunshot wounds, and 32 possible gunshot wounds in 148 bodies. The most frequent sites were torso, 112; legs, 91; head and neck, 31; and arm, 27. 9. CR-3 shows half the total number of gunshot wounds seen in CR-12, 261 versus 422. 10. In the 48 bodies where gunshot wounds were found --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, it says "48". You mean in the 148?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In the 148 cases where gunshot wounds were found, there were between one gunshot wound, 89 bodies, and eight gunshot wounds, one body. The average number of gunshot wounds in the bodies found with gunshot wounds was 1.5, that is, between one and two. There was no significant trend in the directions of the bullet tracks. That is, I could not tell you whether they had been shot from in front or behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could show that to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: 12. There were many post-mortem tampering injuries of the skull, ribs and pelvis, which would tend to obscure pari-mortem, that is, injuries occurring around the time of death, in these regions. 13. There were parts of 160 individuals in the grave. Because of the separation of the body parts, these were collected in 383 body bags (see report by Professor Wright). Many of the bodies were incomplete, and it obviously cannot be guaranteed that the body bags are from separate individuals. Because the individual bodies could not be reconstructed, I have given the cause of death for each of the body bags rather than each individual. It is possible that a divided individual, for example, a separated head and torso and legs, might be given more than one cause of death. In 103 body bags -- sorry. The contents of 103 body bags had an injury in a body part sufficient to cause death due to gunshot wounds in the individual from which the body part came. Thirteen of the body bags had an injury in a body part which would probably cause the death of the individual due to gunshot wounds. Fifteen body bags had an injury in a body part which could possibly cause the death of the individual due to gunshot wounds. Two body bags had injuries in the body parts consistent with the cause of death of gunshot wounds in the individual. And 254 body bags had an undetermined cause of death. Many of these were isolated body parts, or commingled body parts, or incomplete body parts in a general body bag. Of the 35 essentially complete bodies, 29 had a cause of death of gunshot wounds, while six remained with an undetermined cause of death. In my opinion, these six cases probably represent perforated gunshot wounds in soft tissue which can no longer be recognised because of the loss of soft tissue and the absence of bony injury. 15. Identifying documents were found on or near 12 bodies, either at the site or on searching at the mortuary. That completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, thank you. Let's continue taking a tour of this particular report, because you said the format is the same. I see, following your summary, there's an introduction. Can you briefly describe what's in the introduction of each of these reports?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The introduction describes the transfer of the bodies to me and also describes the numbering system used throughout the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you turn to page 4 of your report, because that is a description of the staff members that assisted you in the 1998 autopsies. Would you put that on the ELMO, please. Now, was this a multinational staff that was assisting you, Dr. Lawrence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I had at least 14 different nations represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we start with the pathologists, can you identify the nations from which these pathologists came?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Dr. Bentley is currently working as a forensic pathologist in North Ireland, Northern Ireland. Dr. Marie Cassidy a very experienced forensic pathologist currently working in Ireland. Andrew Davison is a forensic pathologist working in Edinburgh. I work in Australia. Dr. Walter Marty is a widely-published expert on ballistics who is from Switzerland. Professor Helmut Maxeiner is a professor of forensic medicine at Berlin in Germany. Dr. Yvonne Milewski is the chief medical examiner at the Bronx in New York. Alain Miras is forensic pathologist from France. Fritz Priemer is a forensic pathologist from Germany. Dr. Marcus Rothschild is a forensic pathologist again from Berlin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, you were also assisted by autopsy technicians. First of all, can you define what the role of an autopsy technician was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The autopsy technicians basically assisted the forensic pathologist and did a lot of the handling of the bodies from out of and into the morgue. They also processed some of the clothing and generally assisted the pathologist in completing their report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a multinational group of people as well?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. In amongst these, Deborah Brown is from Scotland, as is Ishbel Hunter. Carl Lyon is from Ireland. Robert McNeil is from Scotland. Alfie Moss is from England. Geoff Welburn is from Australia. Paul Woods is from England.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just turn to the category of radiographers. Tell us about, first of all, what they did and where they are from.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The radiographers ran the fluoroscope. That's the mobile X-ray machine. They are technical people who are used to performing X-rays and basically ran and maintained the X-ray equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are they from?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, all of the people shown there are currently working in London. One of them is Irish. I think the rest are all English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And lastly in this group of specialists, there are anthropologists identified in the upper right-hand corner, and we have heard from one of those, Mr. Baraybar, so I don't need you to identify him. But can you identify the others, please, and tell us where they are from?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Carmen Cardoza is Jose's assistant. She's from Peru. Mercedes Doretti is originally Argentinian. She's one of the heads of the Argentinian Missing People Programme in New York. Shuala Martin is a postgraduate student in the United States who has worked on, I think, three or four missions for the United Nations. Amy Powers -- sorry, Julie Powers and Amy Schilling are postgraduate students from the University of New Mexico. Vincent Stefan is a postgrad student who's just about completed his Ph.D. in forensic anthropologist and does all of the forensic anthropology for the office of the investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without identifying where these people are from, there's a category of people as "Data Entry". What did they do?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Their main job was to transform the written reports into typed reports, but they also collated the reports, chased up the signatures, and prepared some of the documents for handover of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your logistics officer is identified. What was his role?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: His job was to basically provide us with things like scalpels and gloves in a country where it was quite difficult to maintain supplies. Forensic work requires a lot of disposables, and his job was to supply us with gloves and all the other equipment required to do the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going through the remaining people and their identities and their nationalities, I take it they also were multinational.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. The crime scene officers were principally Dutch, but there were Australians amongst them. My interpreter was Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next significant part of your report is a section that deals with the procedures of the autopsy. That starts at page 5 of your report. Since you've testified already about the procedure, I'm not going to ask you to repeat that. So carrying on with your report, then you have a section devoted to the autopsy findings, is that correct, which is the section dealing with the minimum number of individuals, the age of the individuals, the sex of the individuals, and the description of the injuries?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it in that section where you outline your findings in greater detail in respect of the human remains examined from this particular site?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I've given -- some of the material is anthropological and is included really to make sense of the results I had. The injuries section basically discusses the problems associated with distinguishing injuries that have occurred before death to those that occur at the time of death from those that occurred after death. It then discusses the gunshot wounds. I have included a number of tables demonstrating what we found. This is on page 9 of the report. What we have here is a description of where we found the gunshot wounds in the 148 bodies. You can see there were 25 definite gunshot wounds in the head and neck, nine in the -- sorry, 93 in the torso, 24 in the arms, and 83 in the legs, with a total of definite gunshot wounds of 255.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two hundred twenty-five?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, 225. I can't read. Table 2 on page 9 shows the number of gunshot wounds in each of the bodies. You can see that they range from 1 to 8. We have a lot with just 1, and then a smaller number above that. The average -- if you look at the average of the bodies that actually had gunshot wounds, the average is 1.8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to your third table under this aspect of your reports found on page 10.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: We attempted to tell the direction from which the people had been shot. Now, given that all but one of these was a secondary site and we were dealing with quite disrupted bodies, this was relatively difficult. We can see, if we look at gunshot wounds from the front to the back, there were 32 that we thought were definitely from front to back; 31 from back to front; but a very large number, 198, where we couldn't tell for certain whether it was from front or back. Similarly, a fairly even distribution between the right-hand and left-hand side of the body, with a moderate number in the midline, and, again, we could not tell direction upwards or downwards in very many of the cases. A vast majority, we couldn't tell. My conclusion from that is that we really -- there are so few we can tell that I don't think you can gain any useful information from that data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in all of your reports there appears to be a diagram. You will see it on the next page. Will you tell us what this represents, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you move that ELMO.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Thanks. This is a composite picture that I created from looking at the X-rays, the diagrams, and the descriptions of the gunshot wounds, and I have effectively placed all of the gunshot wounds onto one body in an attempt to see whether there is a pattern of distribution of the gunshot wounds, and I cannot see a definite pattern to the gunshot wounds. I should point thought that where we knew the direction was from the back, they have been shown on the posterior diagram. The front diagram shows both those that we know the direction of and those we don't know the direction of just in order to show roughly where they occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Lawrence, would you turn to the next page, please, and explain what that table represents. If we could focus down on table 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, perhaps you could assist the witness in focusing down on the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be done for you, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Just zoom it down on to the diagram. Okay. Basically, this shows the projectiles recovered from this scene. It's again a summary of the total number recovered. We found 88 complete or essentially complete bullets; 155 bullet fragments which weren't further specified; 57 jacket fragments, these were copper jacket fragments; and 35 lead fragments which appeared to come from the core of the bullet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, would you turn to page 13 of your report then. This is a chart that continues over to page 14 as well, but this is illustrative of this point that I'd like to make. What is this particular portion of this table?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is a summary of all of the ligatures or potential ligatures which were found at the site or in the autopsy suite. What I have described is the number, the body bag number that the material came from; a rough description of the material it was made of; the dimensions in width; the circumference of the loop; the number of loops, and the location. You will note that 25 of these were associated with the hands, 8 were associated with the body but not obviously around the hands, and 4 were found loose in the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, turn to page 15 of your report, please. Did you create a similar table for blindfolds that were recovered from the bodies from CR-03?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. This is the table that I prepared for the potential blindfolds. Again, the body bag number, the material it was made of, the width, the circumference of the loop, and the location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next section of your report you can see just at the bottom of that ELMO image deals with the cause of death. What is described in that particular section?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: The cause of death section starts with the intrinsic problem in dealing with extensively broken-up skeletal remains; that is, how do you describe the findings in bodies that are not complete? In bodies that are complete, you can assess the whole of the body and reach a conclusion as to whether or not you have a cause of death. If, for example, a body is broken in half, we have the upper half of the body and we have the lower half of the body, and we are unable to relate them together. We've got a very large number of potential victims; they are broken up. We were, in general, fairly unsuccessful in being able to relate one part with another part. We did have occasional successes, mostly related to the identification of clothing on the upper part and lower part, and occasionally where there was a condition present which was identified in both, for example, our gentleman with the very short forearm, we were able to associate with other malformations of the body, but in general, we were not able to match up the top halves and bottom halves. Now, the pathologist would be given a body bag and would attempt to reach a cause of death on that particular body bag. Now, the consequence of this is that you might, for example, in our hypothetical body that's divided in half, have a cause of death in the bottom half and a cause of death in the top half, which would end up with two causes of death in one body. Now, there is really no way -- unless you can relate every body part to every other body part, there is really no way of getting around this problem. The situation is much easier in the intact bodies because you don't have this problem. So I have listed the causes of death in the broken-up body parts in order to describe the injuries present, but it's a kind of difficult figure to understand. So what I've also included is the causes of death in the intact bodies, and I think this is an easier figure to work with because it actually means something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, thank you. Let's continue the tour of your report then. If you'd turn to page 18. I'd like you to tell the Judges what you also included in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There's a description of the clothing that was found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you put that on the ELMO, Dr. Lawrence, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: We were obviously looking for items of military clothing. In this site, there was one body wearing a Yugoslav National Army jacket and a blue uniform which did not appear to have definite military insignia. We also had one body which was carrying an unfired round or cartridge in the jacket pocket. There were no other -- there was no other evidence of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you note in your report any identifying documents that you recovered from the bodies?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. We had a number of documents which would give a provisional identification. Again, you can see here the body bag number; what the item was; the name and family name of the individual; if I could tell the date of birth; and if it was a pass, the numbers on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn now to page 19 of your report. There's an extensive table which continues for many, many pages, Dr. Lawrence. I want to ask you some questions about this. First of all, what is this table?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This is, if you like, the summary of every body bag that we received. This is -- I've attempted to be as open and transparent as I can in showing what we had to deal with. Now, what I've described is the "Body Number." Now, where the body has multiple gunshot wounds, each one of those is given a separate listing. So, for example, in the top one, B319, there were two gunshot wounds, so we've got 319.1 and 319.2. Now, the "Parts Present." When the exhumation was done, the loose bones, those that could not be associated with any other bones, were collected and placed in what were general body bags; that is, they might contain bones from a number of individuals which could not be obviously related to other body parts. Now, in this particular general body bag there were identifiable gunshot wounds in the head and a possible gunshot wound in the left scapula. Now, in my opinion, the gunshot wound in the head would be a cause of death. So we have given a cause of death in that general body bag because that skull had been shot. Now, if we just go a bit further down, you can see the gap below "General Body Bag" is because 319.2 also came from that general body bag. There was no cause of death given on the gunshot wound to the scapula because it was not felt that was a definite cause of death. If we go down now we can see, at 322, this consisted of legs. There were no identifiable gunshot wounds, and the cause of death was undetermined. 323 was a head, letter "H"; arms, the letter "A"; and chest. Now, in this there was a gunshot wound in the left thorax and a cause of death was given as gunshot wound to the thorax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, we won't go through all of this report but there are a number of terms I'd like you to define. For example, "not ascertainable," and that appears in the "Cause of Death" column. There's "not ascertainable," "undetermined," "probable gunshot wound," and "possible gunshot wound." Can you explain those terms?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I was dealing with a number of people from different jurisdictions. A lot of my training is American based, and I tend to use the term "undetermined." A lot of the British pathologists use the term "unascertained," "unascertainable," or "not ascertained." For veracity, I have written down what the pathologist who handled the case called it, not what I would call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly in your report, Dr. Lawrence, I would like you to refer to page 30 of your report, and I'd like you to put that table on the ELMO, and I'd like you to explain what that table represents.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: This table shows all of the features in all of the bodies that we observed that might assist in identifying the individual if once the process of reconciliation with the information from the living is complete; that is, for example, individual number 319 had had a previous shrapnel injury, a healed shrapnel injury in the left hip, so with other information this might lead to identification of this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one would find in here the shortened ulna, for example, that you described?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: We would find all of the old injuries described. We would find all the disabilities, the man with the fused spine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see also there are artefacts such as hearing-aids and --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- tin boxes and the like.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I won't go through all of your comprehensive reports, Dr. Lawrence, but what I would like you to do, please, in respect of the eight reports that you did prepare, I'd like you to summarise your findings to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: To summarise all of the graves that I dealt with in 1998, there was a minimum number of individuals of 883; there were 2.239 body bags; there were 254 relatively intact bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me interrupt you right there. Two hundred and fifty-four relatively intact bodies. All but one of the sites that you examined were sites that -- where the bodies had been removed from another location and reburied?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is a number of intact bodies consistent with the removal bodies from one site to another?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: It's consistent with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue with your findings.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Now, based on the anthropological evidence, there were 7 children, that is, people between the ages of 8 and 13; 48 teenagers; 96 young adults. The bulk of the people were over the age of 25, approximately 688. At the other end of the range, there were 12 between the ages of 55 and 65, and there were at least 9 over the age of 65. Of the 883 individuals, 686 were identifiable as male and 197 were not determined. There were 1.307 definite gunshot wounds. There were 6 shotgun wounds, 25 shrapnel wounds. Now, of those 25 shrapnel wounds, 24 of them were in one site; that was Zeleni Jadar number 5. The largest number of gunshot wounds in a body was 11. The cause of death in the essentially intact bodies, the 254 essentially intact bodies, 203 had gunshot wounds, 1 had died of gunshot wounds and shrapnel wounds, and 55 had an undetermined cause of death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifty or 55?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry, 50 [Realtime transcript read in error "55"] had an undetermined cause of death, and that includes 13 where they were probable or possible gunshot wounds. Ligatures, there were 53 definite ligatures associated with the arms and potentially as many as 83. Blindfolds, there were 44 definite blindfolds and potentially as many as 103. And possibly identifying documents were found on 53 bodies, either at the site or at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded my examination of Dr. Lawrence. In the transcript there is an error. Sorry, Mr. President. The witness corrected --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The transcript is in error on 13:26:46. I asked the witness whether it was 50 or 55. The witness answered "50" and the transcript still reflects "55." So on the question of -- I can ask the witness one more time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, insofar as the number of individuals who had an undetermined cause of death, how many individuals did that represent?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: There were 50 individuals with an undetermined cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, do you have -- I'm sure you have many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, not that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us see how we go, and we'll have a break somewhere along the line. Dr. Lawrence, you shall now be answering questions put to you by Defence counsel Visnjic. Cross-examined by Mr. Visnjic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Lawrence. Dr. Lawrence, most of my questions will be referring to the autopsies linked to the Zeleni Jadar grave site; that is to say, Zeleni Jadar 05.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the evidence presented by the Prosecution to the Court, this site is termed a secondary grave site in comparison to the primary grave site of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of your report, you provide a table which represents the number of injuries from firearms and shrapnel on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind a statement made by your colleague Dr. Clark, I assume that you are dealing with the minimum number of injuries from a bullet or gun or shrapnel on the bodies.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In those cases with shrapnel wounds, we've described all of the bodies where we identified actual possible shrapnel wounds. It is, of course, possible, given the decomposition, that some of the injuries and some of the shrapnel had been lost from the body. So, yes, it is probably a minimum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that this same question would be to whether this is the case with the injuries caused by projectiles. Does that apply there too?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I think I am a little less conservative than Dr. Clark, but, yes, I think there were probably more gunshot wounds than we're reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, when you introduced your associates, you said you had a pathologist who had many reports on ballistics published.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the injuries and the wounds caused by the shrapnel and the remnants you found in the bodies of the victims, were you able to ascertain perhaps the type of firearm used, the type of weapon used; not in detail, but generally speaking, the type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: In general, the type of injuries were those caused by a medium, high-powered rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in the case of shrapnel, the shrapnel you found?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I am a forensic pathologist with some working knowledge of ballistics. I don't have working knowledge of ordnance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, in one body you found fragments of some safety glass, and I suppose it was glass from a vehicle, an automobile.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation for that perhaps?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I do have an explanation. I understand that in the Kravica warehouse, there were a number of parts of cars. I assume that the safety glasses probably come from one of those vehicles, although I guess fragments of safety glass might be found incidentally in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what depth was the safety glass found with respect to the surface of the body?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: If I might -- I'm not sure I know that. I didn't do the actual autopsy. If you give me one moment, I will just ... It's described as being found in the pelvis. I'm sorry I can't be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the position that the glass was found, the place it was found in the pelvis, as you say, embedded in the pelvis, does that perhaps indicate that the body hit an object which was moving at a high speed, in view of the spot where the glass had become embedded?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you just repeat the first part of that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the spot that the glass was found, as far as I was able to see, you found it embedded in bone. Is that correct, glass embedded in bone?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: No. My understanding is it was found in the pelvis in the soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Well, if we take that to be the case, is it possible that the glass got to the place it was found through the impact of the body with an object having the glass, a strong impact?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I guess it's a possibility. I had always viewed it as being -- the glass being accelerated into the body, the opposite way. But I can't exclude it. I don't remember seeing major tears of the soft tissue over it to suggest that it had struck an object, so my assumption was that it was glass that was accelerated into the body rather than the body accelerated against an object.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, can a particle of glass penetrate the skin, perforate the skin, if it is, say, on the floor of a room of some kind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the number of injuries in this last grave site and the number of shrapnel injuries, in particular, in keeping with that, this Zeleni Jadar 05 grave site, does it differ in any way from the primary and secondary grave sites that you examined?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. In this site, we found 24 shrapnel wounds. We only found one other shrapnel wound amongst the other seven graves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, in case of conflict, that is to say, combat operations between two sides, the assumption is that if the two sides are facing each other in a sort of front-line position, that most of the injuries would be caused through a projectile entering the body from the front?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the case of having a group of people in an encirclement under siege, would this assumption be brought into question? That is to say, if the combat operations were such that the people were coming under crossfire, would, according to your experience, this assumption be seriously jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can help you on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I have just one more question. May I take a minute to confer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following on from my last question, can you tell us, in a situation that I tried to describe a moment ago, where would most of the injuries be located on the bodies as a consequence of this type of conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: An encirclement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I think they could be anywhere around the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Dr. Lawrence, during your examination-in-chief, you have dealt with most of the things that were not clear in the testimonies of the previous witnesses. This was asked you by the Prosecution. Therefore, the Defence has no further questions of this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, I only have one question. Re-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reference was made to the Zeleni Jadar site, and I was going through this report and I've realised that I failed to ask you one question. In the Cancari road report that you prepared, we put on the ELMO the staff and you identified various members of the staff. In looking at the staff used in the Zeleni Jadar autopsy reports, there appear to be, for example, 11 pathologists as opposed to 10 pathologists on the Cancari road autopsies, and some of the names of the pathologists appear to be different. Am I correct in saying that in each report you identify the staff members that participated in the examination of the human remains from the particular site?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The people would come from between two weeks to a month. Each of the sites would usually have different personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I have no additional questions, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [In English] I can still say good morning, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said something which struck me. You said you were less conservative than Dr. Clark. What does that mean in your field?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: What it means was that I included in my reports possible injuries and probable injuries. Now, in part, that was because John was dealing with primary graves and I was dealing almost entirely with secondary graves. So I was dealing with cases that were more broken up and so therefore more difficult to interpret. As well, I took the view -- I mean this discussion about gunshot wounds in the thigh came up, the leg. My view was that if left untreated, a gunshot wound that went through the bones of the leg has a relatively high likelihood of killing you if untreated and would give the gunshot wounds in the thigh as a cause of death, given the view that these people were not given transfusions of fluid and were not bandaged and tourniqueted. That's what I mean. I probably listed some injuries that Dr. Clark would probably not have listed as definite gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. For instance, you mention that, just as an example, that 44 were blindfolded and potentially as many as 103. Is that what you call potentially 103?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Well, the 44 are the number that we found -- this is the -- these are the blindfolds, the -- sorry, I'm just -- right. If you're looking at blindfolds, there were 44 where there was evidence either at the site or at the morgue that these were around the face. Now, we found identical -- well, identical pieces of cloth next to bodies or in the grave. Now, I suspect that if we had been there at the time, we would have seen a lot more blindfolds than 44, but I'm trying here to give you those that I can say are definitely blindfolds and also an estimate of how many there could have been as well. I want to be fair about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then let us come to the ages you mentioned. You say there were seven children between 8 and 13.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you have -- could you determine, with precision, the age of a child? Or let's say not exactly but under 13, over 13?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: That's a question you should probably put to the anthropologists, because they are the ones who formally did the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They did that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: They are the ones who did the identification. They did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you seem to be corroborating it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that they are around that age, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And also the people over 65, you can say that a person is over 60 or under 60?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Age estimation over the age of 50, using the current techniques, is quite difficult. Sometimes you get a better impression from just looking at the development of osteoarthritis and those sorts of things, the loss of bone and so forth. That is, again, an estimate, but I think that you will find that there were -- given the other evidence, the hearing aids and so forth, I think there probably were a number over that age. But, again, this question, the expert on this is the anthropologist, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in an exchange of, let's say, of ideas with Defence counsel, you mentioned that you could not answer his question when he told you what would happen if people are encircled and how they would be wounded and so on. Could you continue this debate?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not claim to be a military expert. I have some understanding of what might happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the light of the wounds that we have at the deaths, could it have happened to people encircled or between -- could it be possible that people between two groups received such wounds?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I think it's possible. Whether it did occur, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I mean in light of your experience in this case.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Again, I was not as successful as Dr. Clark in determining the direction of all of -- from which these all came, so I don't think I can make a strong conclusion as to the direction, and hence I can't tell which -- can't really answer that question from a pathological point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Lawrence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Dr. Lawrence, in your Cancari number 3 report, in table 7 on page 18, this was the provisional identification by documents. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I just wondered if you could explain to me two items in there. One, several times it says "pathology report." That doesn't mean they were carrying a pathology report around, or does it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It does. What would be an example of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I think one of them had a blood count or something. Yeah, it was a report from a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: It's the same thing, basically. It's like a medical letter.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yeah, medical letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The second item in the same column is "Red Cross Letters". Do you happen to know what just the gist of a Red Cross letter would be that several people had, apparently?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean probably somebody else can explain it better, but these were messages that appeared to be transmitted to and from people, to refugees. They had gone through the Red Cross. Now, obviously they had letters from people and to people, so it was sometimes difficult to tell necessarily who was the recipient, and sometimes they might carry letters from more than one individual. But these were the letters that were transferred through the Red Cross to these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Lawrence, I would like to go back to the situation when we spoke about the encirclement. I'm going ahead a bit. Would it be possible to have a situation of gunfire, that people would mutually kill each other under conditions of an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER LAWRENCE
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the customs in this court, but I think in Australian courts I would tell you when I think I'm being dragged out of my area of expertise, and I think I'm being dragged out of my area of expertise here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I asked this question because you said that in that kind of situation, the people in the centre could -- that the gunshots were coming from several directions. But if you shoot from this direction, for the person in the middle the gunshot could go ahead of the person in the middle. I asked you this question because you did give your opinions, but of course I won't insist and I understand your answer fully, Dr. Lawrence, and accept it. Mr. Harmon, have we got any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a number of documents in respect of Dr. Lawrence's testimony and one document in respect of Dr. Clark's testimony that was omitted. In respect of the exhibits introduced through Dr. Lawrence, that would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 260 through 268, and there are B/C/S and French versions as well. The B/C/S versions are marked with the letter "A". The French versions are marked with the letter "B" in respect of those exhibits. I'm informed there are no French translations, however, for 263 and for 266. In addition, we have Dr. Lawrence's CV, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 221, and a diagram that was marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit 259. So there are those exhibits in respect of Dr. Lawrence's testimony. And in respect of Dr. Clark's testimony, if I could, it's with respect to Exhibit 258, which is a photograph of a defect in the back of a skull.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, have you any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, would you take note of the different versions of the documents, and the documents have been accepted into evidence. Dr. Lawrence, that completes your testimony in this International Tribunal. We extend our gratitude to you for having come and for your cooperation with international justice. We wish you every success in your future work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Visnjic, I see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to request that our expert, Mr. Stankovic, also be allowed to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and we should like to thank him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, normally this is the time for our 20-minute break, which means that we would have 10 minutes after the break. The question now is the following: Are we going to take a break now, and do you have something for the other ten minutes left, or are we going to complete our work for today? What do you think, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it would be appropriate to complete our work today if all I have left is ten minutes. So thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're not going to have a break and come back into the courtroom, but we'll go on and tomorrow at 9.30 we will resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 1.55 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
